blog.content:
The Ryzen 5 5600 is one of the most popular choices for a value-focused PC. It has 6 cores and 12 threads, which is plenty for coding tools, a browser full of tabs, and modern games.

It fits AM4 motherboards and uses DDR4 memory, so a complete build around it stays affordable. It does not have built-in graphics, so you will need a separate graphics card to get a picture on screen.

Before buying, check that your motherboard supports it. Many older AM4 boards need a BIOS update first, and the update has to be done before you swap the processor.
blog.do_you_know: The 5600 comes with a basic cooler in the box, so you can build a working PC without buying a separate one.

name: AMD Ryzen 5 5600G
use_case_tags: Coding, Office, Budget Build, Light Gaming

blog.content:
The Ryzen 5 5600G is a 6-core processor with graphics built in. That means you can build a complete PC for study, coding or office work without buying a graphics card at all.

The built-in graphics are good enough for everyday use, video playback and light, older games. They are not meant for modern demanding games.

It uses the same AM4 socket and DDR4 memory as the 5600, so you can add a graphics card later when your budget allows.
blog.do_you_know: Built-in graphics share your RAM, so using faster memory in two matching sticks noticeably helps this processor.

specs.Memory support: DDR4 or DDR5 (depends on the motherboard)

blog.content:
The Core i5-12400F is a 6-core, 12-thread processor that gives strong everyday and gaming performance for its price. It is a common pick for mid-range builds.

The letter F in the name means it has no built-in graphics, so you need a graphics card. It fits LGA1700 motherboards.

One helpful detail: whether you use DDR4 or DDR5 memory depends on the motherboard you pick, not on the processor. A DDR4 board is cheaper, a DDR5 board is more future-proof.
blog.do_you_know: The F at the end of an Intel processor name means there is no built-in graphics. Without the F, the processor can display a picture on its own.

specs.Memory support: DDR4 or DDR5 (depends on the motherboard)

blog.content:
The Core i3-12100F is a 4-core, 8-thread processor aimed at tight budgets. It is fast enough for office work, browsing, online classes and light gaming when paired with a graphics card.

It uses the same LGA1700 socket as the 12400F, so you can start with this one and move to a stronger processor later without changing the motherboard, as long as the board supports it.

It has no built-in graphics, so budget for a graphics card, or choose a processor with built-in graphics if you do not need one.
blog.do_you_know: A processor with more cores is not always faster for everyday tasks. Four fast cores can feel just as quick for browsing and office work.

blog.content:
The Ryzen 5 7600 is a newer 6-core processor on AMD's AM5 platform. It runs at higher speeds than the older 5600 and has basic built-in graphics, which is handy for troubleshooting or for a simple office PC.

AM5 motherboards use DDR5 memory only, so a full build costs more than an AM4 build. In return, the platform is newer and is expected to support future processors.

If you want the cheapest possible build, the 5600 is easier on the wallet. If you want a platform that will last longer, the 7600 is a good starting point.
blog.do_you_know: AM5 boards only accept DDR5 memory. DDR4 sticks will not fit, so old RAM cannot be reused.

blog.content:
This is a classic 16GB DDR4 kit made of two 8GB sticks. Two sticks working together give better speed than one, which is why kits are the usual choice.

The heat spreader is low, so it fits under large CPU air coolers that would block taller memory. That makes it an easy, safe choice for many builds.

It is a good match for the Ryzen 5 5600 or Core i5-12400F on a DDR4 motherboard.
blog.do_you_know: Low-profile memory exists because some big CPU coolers hang over the first RAM slot and would not fit a tall heat spreader.

blog.content:
Kingston's FURY Beast is a 16GB DDR4 kit that runs at 3200 MHz. It is built to work with a wide range of Intel and AMD systems and is easy to set up.

By default, memory may start at a slower standard speed until you turn on its rated speed in the BIOS settings (often called XMP or DOCP). Turn it on to get the full 3200 MHz.

It is a straightforward upgrade for any desktop that uses DDR4.
blog.do_you_know: Memory often runs slower than its label until you enable its speed profile in the BIOS. Many people never turn it on.

blog.content:
The Ripjaws V is a widely used 16GB DDR4 kit with the same headline numbers as its rivals: two 8GB sticks, 3200 MHz, CL16.

When the numbers are this similar, price, availability and warranty are usually the deciding factors. Compare current listings before choosing.

Check your motherboard's memory support list if you want the smoothest experience, especially on older boards.
blog.do_you_know: The 'D' in a G.Skill part number like F4-3200C16D means it is a two-stick kit.

blog.content:
This is a single 16GB stick with no heat spreader. It is a simple, low-cost way to add memory, especially in office PCs or when you want to leave a slot free for another stick later.

Because it is one stick, it runs in single-channel mode. That can be slightly slower than two matching sticks in tasks that depend heavily on memory speed, like built-in graphics or some games.

It runs at standard voltage, which makes it very compatible with many older systems.
blog.do_you_know: Two 8GB sticks are often a little faster than one 16GB stick because they work together in dual-channel mode.

blog.content:
This 32GB DDR5 kit is aimed at newer platforms like AMD AM5 and some Intel LGA1700 DDR5 boards. 32GB gives you comfortable space for video editing, virtual machines and heavy multitasking.

DDR5 sticks do not fit DDR4 slots, so only buy this if your motherboard uses DDR5. Check the board's specifications first.

Two 16GB sticks in a kit also give you dual-channel speed.
blog.do_you_know: DDR4 and DDR5 sticks have the notch in different positions, so they physically cannot be installed in the wrong slot without force.

blog.content:
Kingston's DDR5 kit offers the same capacity and speed as the Corsair above, with a higher CAS latency of CL40.

The CAS latency is the delay before memory responds, and a lower number is slightly better. In everyday use the difference between CL36 and CL40 at this speed is small, so price often decides.

Like all DDR5, it only works on boards that support DDR5.
blog.do_you_know: A lower CAS latency number means a shorter delay, but speed and capacity usually matter more for everyday work.

blog.content:
The 970 EVO Plus is a well-known NVMe SSD with strong, consistent speeds and a high endurance rating for its size.

It plugs into an M.2 slot on the motherboard, so there are no cables. Check that your board has an M.2 slot that supports NVMe before buying.

It is a great main drive for Windows, programs and games.
blog.do_you_know: TBW means terabytes written. It is the total amount of data the maker says the drive can write during its life. 300 TB is a lot for home use.

blog.content:
The WD Blue SN570 is a popular value NVMe drive. Its read speed matches faster drives, so loading Windows and apps feels very quick.

Its write speed and endurance are lower than premium drives, which hardly matters for everyday use like study, coding and office work.

It uses an M.2 slot, so no cables are needed.
blog.do_you_know: For most people the difference between a 'fast' and a 'very fast' NVMe drive is hard to notice in daily use.

blog.content:
The Kingston NV2 is a budget-friendly NVMe SSD that uses the newer PCIe 4.0 connection. On a PCIe 4.0 slot it can run at its full rated speed.

It works in older PCIe 3.0 slots too, just at the speed that slot allows. That makes it flexible if you plan to upgrade your motherboard later.

It has a shorter warranty than some rivals, so compare the whole package, not just the speed.
blog.do_you_know: Newer PCIe versions are backward compatible, so a PCIe 4.0 drive still works in a PCIe 3.0 slot.

blog.content:
The Crucial MX500 is a 2.5-inch SATA SSD. It is slower than NVMe drives on paper, but still dramatically faster than an old hard drive.

It is the safe upgrade for older desktops and laptops that have no M.2 slot. You only need a free SATA port and a power connector.

If your PC feels slow and still has a hard drive, this kind of drive is often the best first upgrade.
blog.do_you_know: A SATA SSD cannot go faster than about 560 MB/s because that is the limit of the SATA connection itself.
